h: Why winter afternoons are special here
p: Ask anyone who knows Martin Mere and they'll tell you the same thing: try to catch it on a winter afternoon. The whooper swans that fly in from Iceland gather on the mere in their hundreds, and the centre is known for its swan feeds, when the birds crowd in close to the hides and the noise is something else. Pink-footed geese come in great skeins at dusk too, honking overhead as the light fades over the mosslands. It's genuinely one of the great wildlife moments in the North West, and it's on the doorstep of Ormskirk.

That's not to say the rest of the year is quiet. In spring and early summer the young birds start to appear, the reed beds fill with warblers, and the collection areas are full of fluffy ducklings, which is usually where small children want to spend the most time. Summer is the gentlest time to come, with long light evenings and an easy amble round the paths.

Plan on a few hours at least. A pair of binoculars and a flask will keep the grown-ups happy in the hides, while a change of socks for the kids is never wasted out here. Check what talks and events are running on the day, as they shift with the seasons.

For a bigger day, Rufford Old Hall, a lovely Tudor house looked after by the National Trust, is only a short drive away. Burscough has the Leeds and Liverpool Canal running through it if you fancy a towpath stroll, and Southport's Lord Street and seafront are close enough for tea and a bit of seaside fun.
